title: Which side of the plane should you sit on flying to Fuerteventura?
author: Matt
intro: Flying into Fuerteventura from the UK, the left side of the plane usually gives the best view of the island as you land, with the beaches around Caleta de Fuste and the bare brown hills behind them. Here's why, when it changes and which seats to pick.
seo_title: Flying to Fuerteventura: sit on the left (usually)
seo_description: Usually the left side (seat A) for the island as you land at Fuerteventura. Why the trade winds decide it, when it flips, and where to sit flying home.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Best side:** left, seat A
- **Why:** landings usually head north
- **When it flips:** on rare southerly winds
- **Flight time:** about 4 to 4½ hrs

This is guidance, not a guarantee. The wind decides which way planes land, and air traffic control decides the exact route in, so no seat is certain. On most days, though, the odds are on the left.

sections.heading: Why the left side usually wins
sections.text:
Fuerteventura's airport is on the island's east coast, just south of the capital, Puerto del Rosario. Its single long runway runs roughly south to north, close to the shore. The Canaries sit in the north-east trade winds, and planes land into the wind, so on most days aircraft use runway 01, approaching from the south over the resort of Caleta de Fuste and heading north.

On that final approach, the island is on your **left** and the Atlantic is on your right. From an A seat you may see Caleta de Fuste's bay and marina, the coastal road and the bare volcanic hills of the interior. From the right side, you mostly see the sea.

Tip: flights from the UK arrive from the north and usually swing round to line up from the south. Depending on the route, you may also get a look at Lanzarote, Isla de Lobos or the white Corralejo dunes in the far north of the island before you turn.

sections.heading: How the approach usually works
sections.text:
| Wind | Runway used | Best side for the island |
| --- | --- | --- |
| North-east trade winds (most days) | 01, landing heading north | left (seat A) |
| Southerly (uncommon) | 19, landing heading south | right (seat F) |
| Light or changing winds | either | left is still the better bet |

On the less common days when planes land heading south, the approach comes in over Puerto del Rosario, so the town and coast pass below the right side instead. You won't know in advance, so book the left and take what comes.

sections.heading: Which seats to choose
sections.text:
Where you sit along the plane matters almost as much as the side:

- **In front of the wing** gives the clearest view, but those rows often cost more to choose.
- **Behind the wing** is usually the best value, with a clear view down as the plane descends.
- **Over the wing**, the wing and engine block most of the view below.
- **Check the seat map:** some window seats on popular jets don't line up with a window at all.

On a Boeing 737 or Airbus A320, which most airlines use for Fuerteventura, the left window seat is **A** and the right is **F**. If your airline assigns seats for free at check-in, paying to choose is the only way to be sure of a left-side window.

sections.heading: On the way home
sections.text:
Most departures take off towards the north, into the wind, passing Puerto del Rosario. Planes then head north for the UK.

On take-off the island is again on the **left**, and as you climb you may see the north of the island, the Corralejo dunes and Lanzarote ahead. Which side gets the best view after that depends on the turn, so it varies.

Watch out: on afternoon flights home, the sun is often on the left side of the plane for much of the trip, so a right-hand seat can be more comfortable if you'd rather read or sleep.

sections.heading: What you might see
sections.text:
Fuerteventura looks wild from the air, with very little green. On a clear day you might spot:

- **The Corralejo dunes**, a sweep of white sand in the north of the island, now a natural park.
- **Isla de Lobos**, the tiny island just off Corralejo, and **Lanzarote** across the strait beyond it.
- **Caleta de Fuste**, the resort and marina just south of the airport.
- **The Jandía peninsula**, with its long beaches and the Sotavento lagoon, in the far south.

The flight from most UK airports takes around four to four and a half hours, so there's plenty of time to read up before you land.

sections.heading: Planning a trip to Fuerteventura?
sections.text:
Our [Fuerteventura guide](/destinations/fuerteventura) covers when to go, how long to stay and what to see. If you're deciding between islands, our [Lanzarote or Fuerteventura](/blog/lanzarote-or-fuerteventura) post compares the two.

Flying somewhere else in the Canaries? See which side to sit on flying to [Gran Canaria](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-gran-canaria), [Lanzarote](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-lanzarote) or [Tenerife](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-tenerife), or our general guide to [which side of the plane to sit on](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on).

faqs.question: Which side of the plane is best for landing in Fuerteventura?
faqs.answer: Usually the left side, seat A on most holiday jets. Planes normally land heading north into the trade winds, with the island on the left and the sea on the right.

faqs.question: Can you see the Corralejo dunes from the plane?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, depending on the route in or out. They're in the north of the island, so you're most likely to see them as the plane turns before landing or climbs away on the way home.

faqs.question: How long is the flight to Fuerteventura from the UK?
faqs.answer: About four to four and a half hours from most UK airports, a little longer from Scotland and the North.

faqs.question: Can you see Lanzarote from the plane to Fuerteventura?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, on a clear day. Lanzarote is just across a narrow strait to the north-east, and many approaches pass close enough to see it.
